mcqs.question: Why should a bloated system prompt or unnecessarily long retrieved context be treated as a cost problem, not just a latency one?
options: Because most hosted LLM APIs charge per token, so extra tokens in every request become a recurring cost multiplied across every single call at scale
Because longer prompts always make the model factually less accurate
Because token count only affects cost during model training, not at inference
Because APIs charge a flat fee per request regardless of length, so prompt size only affects latency
mcqs.explanation: Per-token pricing means every extra token in a prompt is a real, recurring cost paid on every single call — at production volume, that adds up fast, independent of any effect on latency. Prompt length doesn't inherently reduce accuracy, token costs apply at inference (not just training), and most providers do charge per token rather than a flat per-request fee.

mcqs.question: What makes model routing an effective cost-optimization strategy?
options: It sends every request to the most expensive model to guarantee maximum quality

It sends the majority of requests, which are typically easy, to a cheap fast model, and escalates only genuinely hard cases to an expensive model — cutting average cost while preserving quality on the hard tail
It eliminates the need for any model at all on simple requests
It requires training a single combined model that replaces both the cheap and expensive options
mcqs.explanation: Routing exploits the fact that most real traffic is easy, sending it to a cheap model, while reserving the expensive model for the harder minority — that's what drives the average cost down without sacrificing quality where it matters. It doesn't send everything to the expensive model, doesn't skip inference for simple requests, and doesn't require training one merged model.

mcqs.question: What's the key difference between quantization and distillation as cost-reduction techniques?
options: Quantization compresses an existing model's weight precision; distillation trains a new, smaller model to mimic the larger model's outputs
They are two names for the exact same technique
Quantization can only be applied to training data, never to model weights
Distillation always produces a larger model than the original teacher
mcqs.explanation: Quantization reduces numeric precision of an already-trained model's weights, shrinking memory and speeding inference with usually small quality loss; distillation instead trains a separate, smaller student model from scratch to approximate the teacher's behavior. They're distinct techniques (not the same thing), quantization operates on weights (not training data), and distillation produces a smaller model by design.

mcqs.question: Why does aggressive request batching make sense for a throughput-sensitive batch workload but not for a latency-sensitive live chat feature?
options: Batching is technically impossible for chat applications
Batching improves cost-per-unit-of-work but adds delay while requests accumulate, which is acceptable when nothing is waiting live but directly hurts perceived responsiveness in chat
Chat workloads never have repeated similar questions, so caching and batching don't apply
Batch workloads cannot use larger, more capable models
mcqs.explanation: Batching trades a bit of added wait time for better throughput and lower per-request cost — fine when no user is waiting live, but directly at odds with the low-latency goal of a chat interface. Batching is technically possible in chat contexts, it's just usually undesirable there; chat workloads often do have repeated questions (which is why caching helps them); and batch workloads can generally afford larger models since throughput, not per-response speed, is the constraint.
